Messi inspires Miami to playoff-clinching victory
item.description:
Lionel Messi set up a Rodrigo De Paul goal and German Berterame snapped his scoring drought as Inter Miami booked their place in the MLS playoffs with a 2-0 win over New York City FC on Wednesday.
Victory gave Cristian 'Kily' Gonzalez his first back-to-back wins since taking over as head coach last month, guaranteeing second-placed Miami at least a place in the wild card round, with five games left to play.
"I'm leaving happy. Obviously, there's a lot to improve, but we're making progress little by little," Gonzalez said.
Messi -- who had scored twice on Saturday after returning to his club side from last week's emotional Argentina send-off -- was again a dangerous presence, playing a hand in both first-half goals.
In the 20th minute Messi trapped the ball just outside the penalty area and passed it to De Paul, who found Suarez on the byline with a diagonal looping ball.
Suarez rolled it flat across the face of the goal, giving Berterame a simple finish for his first goal since May.
De Paul grabbed Miami's second on a quick counter with the final kick of the first half. Berterame brought the ball across the halfway line and was slightly fortunate to find Messi to his right with a mishit pass.
Messi drew in three defenders then laid it off with the outside of his left foot to De Paul, who slammed it high to the keeper's right.
In a goalless second half, Messi sent a curling effort from just outside the box over the bar.
As the game clock hit 90, Messi played a short corner to De Paul, who unleashed a shot from outside the box toward the far top corner. United States national team goalkeeper Matt Freese made a superb diving save, tipping the ball onto the post.
New York City, on a dire streak of just one win in their last 11 MLS games, at least had a chance for a consolation deep in stoppage time with a penalty.
Ian Fray brought down fellow substitute Talles Magno, who turned sharply away from goal and ran into the defender's trailing leg.
But Dayne St. Clair made a brilliant save, flinging himself low and right to palm the ball around the bar.
It was Inter Miami's second straight clean sheet, after none in their previous 10.
"I really liked how we handled dropping back into defensive shape. We didn't get caught out on the counter and were very aggressive, breaking up plays whenever a sudden transition from them looked likely," said Gonzalez.
"Perhaps our ball circulation was a bit too slow at times, but that's just how the game played out."
Even with first-place Nashville out of sight this year in the Eastern Conference, the win consolidated Miami's grip on second, and home-field advantage into the playoffs.

item.title: PSG 'got lucky' to win City thriller, says Luis Enrique
item.description:
Paris Saint-Germain boss Luis Enrique said the European champions rode their luck to beat Manchester City 4-2 and maintain a perfect start to their defence of the Champions League.
The visitors ran riot in the first half of City's first home game since being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules as they raced into a 3-0 lead.
Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha were on target in a near flawless first 45 minutes by the French champions.
But City roared back after the break as Erling Haaland struck twice, while they also hit the woodwork twice and were denied by a brilliant goalline clearance by Nuno Mendes.
"We could have lost this match if they scored the chances that they created," said Luis Enrique.
"I think it was a very nice match, but the way they play, it's amazing. We like to play these kind of matches."
Maghnes Akliouche briefly restored PSG's three-goal lead in the second half, while Ferran Torres also missed a late penalty for the visitors.
"We try to win every single match. We try to score. We don't stop if we score one or two goals," added Luis Enrique.
"It's very nice to feel that but I have to repeat, today we were lucky because in the second half we could have conceded more goals."
Enzo Maresca had made a perfect start to the daunting challenge of replacing Pep Guardiola as City manager by winning his first eight games in all competitions.
Guardiola, who won 20 trophies in a 10-year spell at City, made his return to the Etihad Stadium in a show of support after City were found guilty on more than 100 charges of financial impropriety between 2009 and 2018.
But he saw his former players fall to their first defeat of the season despite a spirited fightback after being thoroughly outplayed in the first half.
"From tonight we can learn many things," said Maresca. "Even if we concede two goals (in two minutes) against the best team in Europe, we need to continue.
"I try to continue to learn from the players because I just arrived three months ago, but the feeling at the moment is very good."
Victory took PSG top of the Champions League table after two games, while City drop to 17th.

item.title: PSG beat City in Champions League thriller, Barcola hits Liverpool hat-trick
item.description:
Reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain romped to a 4-2 victory away to embattled Manchester City in the UEFA Champions League on Wednesday, while Bradley Barcola hit his first Liverpool goals with a hat-trick in a 6-3 win over LASK in Austria.
Elsewhere on a prolific night of European action, Real Madrid came from 3-1 down to beat Roma 4-3 and Aston Villa demolished Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park.
City were playing at home at the Etihad Stadium for the first time since being found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over almost a decade that have left them facing the prospect of severe sanctions.
That verdict appeared to be hanging over the City team as PSG raced into a three-goal lead just past the half-hour mark, with Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha all netting for the French side.
With former boss Pep Guardiola watching on, City produced a second-half fightback as Erling Haaland scored twice to take him to four Champions League goals already this season.
However, PSG got a fourth in between the Norwegian's strikes, with City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma unable to keep out a Maghnes Akliouche shot.
Donnarumma later made some amends by saving a Ferran Torres penalty, but City succumbed by the same margin as in their last Champions League meeting with PSG in January 2025.
"In the first half we were far superior to a great City side," Paris coach Luis Enrique told broadcaster Canal Plus. "You can think these games are over but it is never the case at this level, and we could have ended up losing."
Back-to-back title-holders PSG have won both Champions League games this season, scoring 10 goals in the process. They face Barcelona next week.
"Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more," City coach Enzo Maresca told TNT Sports.
Barcola, a big-money summer signing from PSG, had not found the net for Liverpool before scoring three times at the Raiffeisen Arena after Ronald Araujo had broken the deadlock against the Austrian champions.
Jeremie Frimpong and Lewis Koumas also netted for Andoni Iraola's side, who were 4-0 ahead at one point before LASK scored three times in the space of 15 second-half minutes through Robert Ljubicic and Florian Flecker's brace.
"Obviously I think he has to enjoy this because to score a hat-trick in the Champions League is always very difficult," said Iraola of France forward Barcola.
- Real late show, Villa hit six -
There was a dramatic denouement in Italy, where a Marten de Roon goal and a Donyell Malen brace had Roma 3-1 up against Real Madrid inside the final 10 minutes.
However the visitors, who had earlier seen Kylian Mbappe score on his 100th Champions League appearance, produced an incredible late fightback.
Carlos Espi pulled one back in the 82nd minute and Brazil forward Endrick equalised before Antonio Rudiger grabbed a last-minute winner for Jose Mourinho's men.
Swiss international Johan Manzambi opened the scoring for Villa against Fenerbahce on his 21st birthday, setting his club up for their biggest ever European victory.
Nicolas Jackson scored twice before half-time, and Ross Barkley bagged a second-half brace including a penalty. Tammy Abraham completed the scoring, leaving the Turkish side stunned.
Fredrik Sjovold got the only goal of the game as Norway's Bodo/Glimt beat former European champions Borussia Dortmund 1-0, while Real Betis beat Porto 3-2 in Spain.
Abde Ezzalzouli put Betis ahead just after half-time, only for Gabri Veiga and Samuel Aghehowa to hit back for the Portuguese champions. However, Juan Hernandez levelled again and veteran Isco got a late winner.
In Rotterdam, Feyenoord beat Como 3-2 as the Dutch side's coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst got the better of Cesc Fabregas.
Assane Diao gave the Italians the lead but Gjivai Zechiel and Anis Hadj Moussa struck for Feyenoord before an own goal by goalkeeper Robert Sanchez made it 3-1. Anastasios Douvikas then pulled one back.
Ukraine's Shakhtar Donetsk were playing at home for the first time at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge stadium, and they marked the occasion with a 3-1 win over AEK Athens.
Lovro Majer gave AEK the lead, but a Pedrinho penalty levelled matters before Vinicius Tobias and Gleiker Mendoza sealed the win to leave Shakhtar on four points from two outings.
Stuttgart won 3-0 away to Slovan Bratislava in the night's other game.

item.description:
More than 100 residents of low-income communities in Dhaka North have received equipment to support income-generating activities under a livelihood assistance project aimed at improving economic opportunities for urban poor communities.
A total of 107 residents received sewing machines, information technology (IT) equipment and business carts at a distribution ceremony held at the Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) Auditorium on Wednesday.
The Livelihoods Support for Urban Poor Communities in Bangladesh (LSUPCB) project is implemented by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in partnership with the Local Government Division (LGD), under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives, with financing from the Global Development Fund (GDF) under China's South-South Cooperation.
The initiative aims to strengthen the economic resilience of vulnerable urban households through skills development, entrepreneurship support and livelihood assets, creating income opportunities for women and youth.
In DNCC, the project supports 16 low-income communities through Community Development Committees (CDCs). Beneficiaries receive 3 months of skills training, followed by productive assets based on their skills and business plans.
At the ceremony, 36 beneficiaries received sewing machines for tailoring and home-based businesses, 30 received IT equipment for digital services and technology-based enterprises, and 41 received business carts for small-scale trading.
Addressing the ceremony as the chief guest, DNCC Administrator Md Safiqul Islam Khan said: “These assets are not simply equipment; they are opportunities to build sustainable livelihoods. Beneficiaries must use them responsibly to generate income, strengthen their businesses and create a better future for their families.”
Chairing the event, DNCC Chief Executive Officer Mohammad Ashaduz Zaman said: “Skills development becomes more meaningful when people have the resources to put their training into practice. This support will help beneficiaries turn their abilities into income-generating opportunities.”
Yugesh Pradhanang, international technical adviser and project manager of the Livelihoods Improvement of Urban Poor Communities Project at UNDP Bangladesh, said: “Providing livelihood assets alongside practical training helps people move toward financial independence. Our focus is on enabling vulnerable women and youth to build sustainable livelihoods.”
The LSUPCB project operates across 6 cities and towns in Bangladesh, supporting employment, entrepreneurship and economic self-reliance among vulnerable urban communities.
Mohammad Mamun-Ul-Hassan, deputy secretary and chief social welfare and slum development officer at DNCC, delivered the welcome address.
Through government and development partnerships, the initiative seeks to strengthen household incomes, promote small-scale entrepreneurship and create sustainable economic opportunities for urban poor communities.

item.title: Durga Puja preparations going on in full swing in Tangail
item.description:
Preparations for Durga Puja are in final stages across Tangail, with artisans working day and night to complete idols and organisers putting the finishing touches to pandals ahead of the Hindu community’s biggest religious festival.
This year, 1,356 pandals will host the festival across the district’s 12 upazilas, 110 more than last year. However, artisans say soaring raw material prices and shrinking profits are making it increasingly difficult to sustain their livelihoods.
Durga Puja will begin nationwide on October 15 with Maha Panchami and conclude on October 21 with Bijoya Dashami and the immersion of idols.
Artisans are racing against time to complete idols of Goddess Durga and her children — Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartik and Ganesha. While idol-making has been completed in many places, work continues at several others, with artisans painting idols and adding the final touches to meet deadlines.
From early morning until late at night, workers are putting in long hours as preparations gather pace and the festive atmosphere spreads across the district.
According to traditional Hindu beliefs, Goddess Durga will arrive on an elephant and depart by boat this year.
Despite the increase in the number of pandals, idol-makers say rising prices of clay, paint and other materials have significantly eroded their profits. They also say their earnings are no longer sufficient to cover household expenses.
Pradip Chandra Pal, an artisan who has been making idols for 20 years, said preparations were now at their busiest, with workers labouring day and night to finish their work.
“The cost of everything needed to make idols has increased. A colour that used to cost Tk100 now costs Tk150. The price of clay has also risen significantly,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
Pal said he had made 10 idols this year at a cost of Tk150,000 and expected to sell them for around Tk250,000.
“Earlier, we could spend six months without work after making idols for Durga Puja. Now, that is no longer possible,” he said, adding that rising costs and low returns had made the profession increasingly difficult.
Another artisan, Arnab, who has been in the profession for seven years, said the workload increased sharply ahead of the festival, leaving little time for rest.
“We hardly have any time to rest during this period. But the money we earn from painting idols is not enough to run our households,” he said.
The artisans called for government assistance to help them cope with rising production costs and declining profits.
Tangail District Puja Celebration Committee Acting President Chitta Ranjan Sarkar said organisers had held discussions with representatives of all puja committees to ensure the celebrations proceeded smoothly.
He attributed the increase in the number of pandals to the administration’s overall cooperation.
“Police will be deployed at every pandal, alongside CCTV surveillance and other security measures. We hope to complete the celebrations without any untoward incidents,” he said.
Tangail Superintendent of Police Mohammad Shamsul Alam Sarkar said a special security plan had been drawn up for the festival.
Police, Detective Branch personnel and plainclothes officers will be deployed to maintain law and order, he said, adding that the police would remain vigilant to ensure peaceful celebrations.

item.description:
The fourth session of the current parliament will begin on November 9 next (Monday), according to a notification issued by the Parliament Secretariat on Wednesday.
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has summoned the session to be held at 3:30pm on the day at the Parliament Building in the capital.
The president summoned the session in exercise of the powers conferred upon him under Article 72(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, said a notification signed by Md Monir Hossain, director of the Public Relations Sub-division-1 of the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat.
This will be the fourth session of the current parliament constituted following the latest general election held on February 12, 2026.
With this, the 13th parliament is going into the session after a 60-day recess as the third session was prorogued on September 10 last after only nine sittings.
Earlier, the second session, also known as the budget session, was prorogued on July 15 after 27 working days. During that session, Parliament passed the Tk938,000-crore national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, the first budget under the current BNP government.

Indonesia haze spikes Singapore pollution, shuts East Timor schools
item.description:
Air pollution in part of Singapore hit the country’s “very high” band on Wednesday while East Timor shut schools, as haze from forest fires raging in Indonesia causes a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore on Wednesday hit “very high” -- the country’s top level -- the National Environment Agency said.
It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic meter, vastly exceeding the World Health Organization’s recommended average annual exposure of five micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday, and as far afield as the Philippines.
The closures in East Timor were necessary “as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions,” the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore’s National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
“It’s a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside,” a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
“With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier,” the 27-year-old said.
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother -- also masked -- for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
“Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler,” Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland, and when the wind shifted, the flames moved towards their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
“My house is gone,” Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything,” said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.
The haze has prompted Malaysia to request a meeting of regional body Asean, and on Tuesday Malaysian parliamentarian Syed Saddiq Rahman urged a “diplomatic protest.”
“We must send a diplomatic protest note, not just on behalf of Malaysia, but Asean. You need to treat them as an outcast in the region,” he said.

item.title: British delegation discusses gender violence, land rights in Sylhet
item.description:
A British parliamentary delegation has discussed issues ranging from gender-based violence and land rights to visa services and international flight connectivity during its visit to Sylhet, as part of a week-long trip to Bangladesh.
The delegation from the British All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) held the engagements in Sylhet from October 9 to 11, focusing on education, employment, infrastructure, land disputes, and visa and consular services.
Before arriving in Sylhet on Friday, October 9, the delegation held high-level meetings with officials and representatives of Bangladesh’s government, Parliament and civil society in Dhaka, and with the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Cox’s Bazar.
Upon arrival, the delegation met representatives of BRAC, visited Sylhet Kidney Foundation Hospital and held roundtable discussions at the BRAC Learning Centre.
Participants in the roundtable included Sylhet Administrator Abdul Qayyum Chowdhury, Sylhet Women Chamber of Commerce President Lubana Yesmin Shampa, District Commissioner Abdullah Al Mamun and Sylhet Press Club President Moktabis Nur.
On October 10, the delegation participated in roundtable consultations organized by the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST). Members met representatives of the Sylhet Bar Association, legal experts and tea garden workers.
Discussions focused on violence against women and girls and legal redress, labor rights and working conditions, minority group advocacy and community action.
In the afternoon, the delegation visited the Urang (Oraon) community with BRAC to learn more about issues affecting Indigenous and minority Hindu communities in the region.
The delegation also met participants in BRAC’s Ultra Poor Graduation Program to learn about development initiatives in Sylhet.
On October 11, the delegation visited BLAST’s Sylhet unit and met judicial officials, lawyers and paralegals. Discussions covered legal aid and access to advocacy and advice.
The delegation’s visit was supported by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association UK (CPA UK).

item.title: Fire breaks out at drug factory in Tongi
item.description:
A fire broke out at the pharmaceutical factory of Drug International Limited in Cherag Ali area of Tongi, Gazipur, on Wednesday morning.
The fire started around 10am on Wednesday, prompting the deployment of 10 fire service units to bring it under control.
Three units initially responded to the scene under the leadership of Senior Station Officer Shahin Alam. The number of units was gradually increased due to the intensity of the fire.
Talha Bin Jasim, an official of the Media Cell of the Fire Service and Civil Defence Directorate, confirmed that 10 units, including three from Tongi Fire Service, were working to control the blaze.
The cause of the fire and how it started remain unknown.

item.title: Son kills mother, critically injures father in Kurigram
item.description:
A woman was killed and her husband critically injured after their son allegedly stabbed them at their home in Kurigram Sadar upazila early Wednesday.
The incident occurred around dawn in Belgachha Union, Officer-in-Charge of Kurigram Sadar Police Station Kamal Hossain confirmed the incident.
The deceased was identified as Munira Begum, 56. Her husband, Sardar Ali, 65, a retired textile engineer, sustained serious injuries and was taken to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
Their son, Mostakin Alam Shovon, 35, allegedly carried out the attack before fleeing the scene.
According to police and local residents, Shovon, who was reportedly addicted to drugs, had been sent to rehabilitation centres several times by his parents but repeatedly escaped. His parents were preparing to send him to a centre again, but he refused to go.
Staff from a rehabilitation centre in Sirajganj had arrived at the family's home early Wednesday to take Shovon to the facility.
Realising their intention, Shovon came out of his room and stabbed his mother in the chest with a knife. When his father intervened, Shovon stabbed him repeatedly in the abdomen before fleeing.
The rehabilitation centre staff rescued the injured couple and took them to Kurigram General Hospital, where the on-duty physician declared Munira dead. Ali was later referred to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.

CCGP approves Tk1,466 C fertilizer imports from 4 countries
item.description:
The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase (CCGP) on Wednesday approved the import of fertiliser worth around Tk1,466 crore from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Russia and Canada to meet the country’s agricultural demand.
The approval was given at a meeting chaired by Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury.
The recommendations cover imports of urea, muriate of potash (MOP) and diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertilisers under government-to-government (G2G) agreements and existing contracts.
Under the proposals, 40,000 tons of bulk granular urea fertiliser containing 10% nitrogen will be imported from Saudi Arabia’s SABIC Agri-Nutrients Company for Tk220.65 crore. The price has been set at US$ 446.67 per ton.
The committee also recommended importing 42,000 tons of bulk granular urea fertiliser from Fertiglobe Distributions Limited of the UAE for Tk275.78 crore at $531.67 per ton.
Both urea consignments will be imported in the 2026-27 fiscal year.
The committee recommended importing 35,000 tons of MOP fertiliser from Russia’s JSC Foreign Economic Corporation (Prodintorg) for Tk166.10 crore at $383.80 per ton under a G2G agreement between the Russian company and the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC).
It also recommended two separate imports of 40,000 tons each of MOP fertiliser from the Canadian Commercial Corporation (CCC) under G2G agreements with BADC. Each consignment will cost Tk188.90 crore, with the price fixed at $382.38 per ton.
The proposals allow for an additional 10% over the specified quantities.
In another proposal, the committee recommended importing 40,000 tons of diammonium phosphate fertiliser from Saudi Arabia’s MA’ADEN for Tk 425.58 crore under an agreement with BADC.
The DAP fertiliser will cost $861.50 per ton and forms the fifth lot of the 2026 supply arrangement.
The imports are intended to ensure the availability of fertilisers required by farmers for agricultural production.

Pope Leo has cancerous tumour removed in lung operation
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and "woke up normally" after the procedure, the Vatican said.
A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread.
"To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed," the Vatican said in a statement.
The operation "confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests", it said.
The 71-year-old pope was in the operating room at Rome's Gemelli hospital for a total of three hours and the operation lasted half that time.
"The surgery was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said, with a source adding that he had requested dinner after the procedure.
Juanita Mora, medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, told AFP that when this type of cancer is "caught in early stages, then it has a very, very good prognosis".
She said much would depend on the stage of the cancer found and whether it had spread.
In cases of surgical removal and when the cancer is caught early and localised, five-year survival rates from lung adenocarcinoma were "80 to 98 percent", she said.
"They'll determine if he needs chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy for the adenocarcinoma," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a practicing Catholic, said after the surgery that he and his wife were "united in prayer for (Leo's) health following his recent diagnosis".
"May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," Rubio said on X.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his "thoughts and prayers" were with the pontiff, calling him "a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world".
Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday hours before the surgery.
He is staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation.
The Vatican has said it expects the recovery to take a week.
His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.
The surgery marks Leo's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered a nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.
The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.
Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope's condition.
Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried.
"However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors," she said.
"I will pray a lot for him."
Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned.
"He's still quite young and I really wasn't expecting this. I thought he was in better health," he said, noting that "thankfully it was caught in time".
The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican.
Dozens of people attended, and Reina asked all the city's parishes to join in.
The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been "very calm" about his condition when they met on Monday.
The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope's lungs.
Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.
He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

item.title: Prof Yunus’ harassment in US: New York Mission asked to take due legal action
item.description:
Strongly condemning the harassment of former interim government Chief Adviser Professor Dr Muhammad Yunus at John F Kennedy Airport in New York, US, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has asked its Mission in New York to take up the matter with local law enforcing agencies.
The MoFA, in a statement, also said it asked the Bangladesh Mission in New York to identify the perpetrators and take due legal action against those who have tarnished the image of Bangladesh and all its citizens before the world.
“The government of Bangladesh strongly condemns the harassment of former interim government chief adviser Professor Dr Muhammad Yunus at John F Kennedy Airport in New York, US,” said the ministry.
It appears that a group of perpetrators suspected to be linked with the Bangladesh Awami League, were behind this harassment committed against Nobel Peace Prize laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus on foreign soil, the government said, noting that Prof Yunus is highly respected by the international community.
Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said the government will take necessary measures over the harassment of Prof Yunus.
Any attempt by Awami League leaders or activists living abroad to engage in such acts would not go unchallenged, he said at a press briefing on the progress of various government activities at Secretariat.
Dr Yunus is currently in the US, where an attempt was made to harass him at an airport, he said, adding that the incident is believed to be linked to Dr Yunus taking responsibility for running the state after Sheikh Hasina fled the country.

Car driven by DU teacher’s son hits 7 students on campus
item.description:
Seven Dhaka University (DU) students were injured after a private car hit them on campus on Tuesday morning.
Six of the injured are from the Department of Marketing and one from the Department of Linguistics. They were taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), where one student was reported to be in critical condition.
The accident occurred around 11am when Sadman Sakib, a student of the university’s Institute of Information Technology for the 2023-24 academic year, was driving the car. He is the son of Dr Md Shahidul Islam, a teacher at the Department of Mathematics.
According to witnesses, Sadman lost control of the car while learning to drive and hit the students. Some were riding in rickshaws, while others were standing near a gate adjacent to the Faculty of Business Studies (FBS) and Mall Chattar.
Following the accident, students detained Sadman and took him to the university proctor’s office.
Sadman said he had taken the car out despite having little driving experience. A driver was accompanying him.
“I drove around the Arts Building once and was approaching FBS when I became frightened after seeing a large crowd. While trying to brake, I mistakenly pressed the accelerator. The car began moving at high speed and hit several students in front of me. The driver later helped bring it under control,” he said.
Eyewitnesses also said angry students beat two people who were in the car and vandalized the vehicle after the accident.
Sadman’s father, Dr Mohammad Shahidul Islam, said he would accept whatever decision the university authorities made regarding the incident.
DU Proctor Associate Professor Dr Md Israfil Ratan said he had been informed of the accident and that arrangements had been made for the injured students’ treatment.
“Some students fell from rickshaws. Arrangements have been made for their treatment. We were fortunate that there was no major accident,” he said.

item.title: Zahed: Legal action to be taken over harassment of Dr Yunus in US
item.description:
Legal action will be taken over the alleged harassment of former interim government chief adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus in the United States, Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman has said.
He said the government would follow the same legal process adopted after actress Azmeri Haque Badhon was harassed in Italy last month.
Zahed made the remarks at a regular press briefing at the Secretariat on Tuesday in response to questions from journalists about the incident involving Yunus.
A video circulating on social media shows Dr Yunus leaving John F Kennedy Airport in New York in a wheelchair, with several people approaching him and shouting slogans. The protesters were heard making abusive remarks, including asking why he had come to the United States.
Supporters of the banned Awami League living abroad have been accused of being involved in the incident.
Responding to questions, Zahed said: “I am aware of the legal process initiated after our actress Azmeri Haque Badhon was harassed. The same will happen in this case. I want to tell the Awami League ‘terrorists’ abroad that if they attempt such actions, it will not go unchallenged.”
The adviser also said the government would examine whether there had been any lapse in the protocol and status accorded to Dr Yunus, who served as chief adviser to the interim government.
Asked about the prospects for political reconciliation, Zahed said he saw no possibility of reconciliation with the Awami League, citing what he described as a lack of remorse among its leaders and their threats.

item.title: Cuet VC confined to office for 21 hours as students lock gate
item.description:
Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CuetT) Vice-Chancellor Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam has remained confined to his office for nearly 21 hours after protesting students locked the administrative building's main gate, demanding the reinstatement of former VC Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem.
The students locked the gate around 12:30pm on Monday, trapping the vice-chancellor and several others inside. Two people accompanying him fell ill and were taken to hospital around midnight.
As of 10am on Tuesday, students were still staging a sit-in in front of the administrative building.
Around 1:30am, reports emerged that two people inside the building had fallen ill. Dr Md Abdullah of the Cuet Medical Centre went to the scene to provide medical assistance.
The two, engineers Shahriar and Titu Mo Sohan, both Cuet alumni, received first aid before being taken to hospital for further treatment.
Asked about his health, Sheikh Shariful Alam said he was doing well.
“Two of our alumni members are suffering from complications related to high blood pressure, so I called for an ambulance and a doctor. Since everyone has been confined here for such a long time, they are feeling unwell and exhausted,” he said.
The vice-chancellor arrived at the Cuet campus in Raozan at 8:45am on Monday and entered the administrative building after breaking the lock on its front door. Students later locked the building’s main gate around 12:30pm. The water and electricity supplies were subsequently cut off.
Sheikh Shariful Alam, a professor at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (Kuet), was appointed Cuet vice-chancellor on September 21.
Students had already been protesting the removal of former vice-chancellor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem and demanding his reinstatement. They have been enforcing a total shutdown since September 22.
University teachers, officers and staff have also been observing a work stoppage over the same demands. As a result, classes, examinations and other academic activities have remained suspended for nearly three weeks.

President stresses public awareness, preparedness to tackle disasters
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Tuesday stressed the need for preparedness, greater public awareness, disaster-resilient infrastructure and stronger early warning systems to mitigate the impact of natural disasters.
The government, relevant institutions and the public must work together to reduce disaster risks, said the president while addressing a programme marking the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction 2026 at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka.
Bangladesh is a disaster-prone country where floods, cyclones, tidal surges, river erosion, landslides, droughts, lightning strikes and earthquakes pose persistent threats to people's lives and livelihoods, he said.
The adverse effects of climate change had further aggravated the situation, he said, adding that although Bangladesh contributed little to global warming, it had to bear a disproportionate share of its harmful consequences.
Referring to the devastating cyclone and tidal surge of 1970, the president said Bangladesh's history demonstrated the catastrophic consequences of natural disasters. “Such events not only claimed lives but also severely damaged livelihoods, the economy, infrastructure and overall development.”
He said disaster risks are increasing worldwide due to climate change, making the situation particularly concerning for vulnerable countries like Bangladesh.
Therefore, instead of focusing solely on disaster-related losses and damage, the country needed to strengthen preparedness and preventive measures well in advance, he added.
The president said Bangladesh has already made significant progress in disaster management.
Improved early warning systems, the establishment of shelters, volunteer networks and increased public awareness help reduce disaster-related deaths, but these initiatives need to be made more effective, he said.
He also drew the attention of the minister concerned to the need for law to ensure the protection of disaster management volunteers and recognise their contributions.
Expressing concern over the risks arising from unplanned urbanisation and weak infrastructure, the President said the potential consequences of an earthquake in Dhaka require particular attention.
Unplanned construction and inadequate urban planning could increase casualties during a major disaster, he said, stressing that the relevant authorities must ensure compliance with building safety regulations and implement proper urban planning.
He also highlighted the importance of maintaining the natural flow of rivers, preventing river pollution, improving drainage systems and protecting the environment to reduce disaster risks.
The ministries and institutions concerned must work in a coordinated manner to address these issues, he said.
Emphasising the role of local communities in disaster preparedness, the President said people in the haor areas of Sylhet demonstrated growing awareness by taking advance precautions and responding to early warnings.
Such initiatives needed to be expanded, he said, urging every family to keep essential documents and emergency supplies in safe places, respond promptly to early warnings and actively participate in disaster management activities.
The president said the government has undertaken various programmes to minimise disaster-related losses, adding that these initiatives must be implemented with sincerity and effective planning to reduce risks before disasters and ensure swift recovery afterwards.
To build a disaster-resilient Bangladesh, every home must be made safe, every family prepared and every community empowered, he said.
He also stressed the need to ensure transparency in development planning and policymaking, protect the environment and incorporate disaster risks into infrastructure development.
Calling for collective efforts to tackle disasters, the President said a resilient Bangladesh could be built through united initiatives, ensuring that people were protected from the impacts of disasters and could recover quickly in their aftermath.
Minister for Disaster Management and Relief Asadul Habib Dulu, State Minister for Disaster Management and Relief M Iqbal Hossain and Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief Munshi Rafiqul Alam were also present at the event.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 8th globally with ‘unhealthy’ air quality
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 8th among the world's most polluted cities on Tuesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 158 at 9:52am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Lahore in Pakistan ranked first with an AQI score of 201, while Singapore in Singapore and Delhi in India ranked second jointly with a score of 196, followed by Hanoi in Vietnam third place with an AQI score of 186.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) said Tuesday that key leaders had been detained after entering an iconic protest site in New Delhi blocked by police.
Opposition parties and supporters of the movement have taken to the streets in recent days, defying a security clampdown to demand the resignation of the head of India’s election commission, accusing it of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Delhi Police said on Monday that Jantar Mantar in the heart of the capital had been taken off the list of designated official protest sites.
The site has been sealed off for several days by yellow metal barricades and guarded by a heavy police presence.
But a video posted online by CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke on Tuesday showed protesters clambering over the barricades, running into the empty space and waving the national flag -- before police chased and detained them.
“CJP sneaks inside to reclaim Jantar Mantar,” the group said in a post on social media, adding that those detained included leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde.
“All of them have been detained by Delhi Police,” it added.
Delhi Police had announced three official sites on Monday as alternatives to Jantar Mantar, where protesters have gathered for decades -- including CJP demonstrations that led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal in July.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” Dipke said, tagging Modi in his post.
Modi, in comments at a business conference in New Delhi on Tuesday, called India the “mother of democracy,” but did not refer directly to the protests.
“In our country, people openly debate a wide range of issues and discuss different perspectives,” he said.

item.title: Iran says ‘deeply concerned’ over escalation between Houthis, Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Iran said Monday it was “deeply concerned” by escalating attacks between Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh’s airport.
“We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told a weekly press conference, adding that Tehran was ready “to help facilitate dialogue between the parties.”
A Houthi strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
“We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries,” Baqaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation “through dialogue and engagement.”
The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed “Axis of Resistance,” a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.

item.title: 303 children live with mothers in prison, report tells HC
item.description:
The Department of Social Services has recommended placing 303 children living with their incarcerated mothers in prisons across the country with close relatives of their choice or in government-run children’s homes, considering their best interests.
In a report submitted to the High Court, the department said the children were regularly monitored through the Offender Reformation and Rehabilitation Association. They were also provided with essential support, including toys, clothing and baby food.
On June 15, the High Court sought a report from prison authorities detailing the number and ages of children living with their mothers in prisons across the country. However, that report has yet to be submitted.
A High Court bench comprising Justice Khizir Ahmed Choudhury and Justice Md Ziaul Haque issued an order and a rule following a writ petition filed by Supreme Court lawyer Kamrun Nahar Mahmud Deepa.
The rule asked why directives should not be issued to take necessary measures to ensure the safety, welfare, education, proper development and fundamental rights of children living in prisons.
Barrister Kamrun Nahar Mahmud Deepa told Bangla Tribune that the Supreme Court was currently in recess and the final hearing on the writ petition would take place after the holidays.
According to Department of Prisons data, 299 children were living with their mothers in the country’s 74 central and district jails as of April 26, 2024. Of them, 153 were girls, and 146 were boys.
Most of the mothers are accused in drug-related cases. Some are serving prison sentences, while others are awaiting trial.
Division-wise, Dhaka accounted for 100 children living with their mothers in prison, followed by Chittagong with 90, Rajshahi with 25, Rangpur with 25, Khulna with 20, Sylhet with 19, Mymensingh with 13 and Barisal with four.
Kashimpur Central Women’s Jail in Gazipur has the highest number of children living with their mothers, according to the report.
While the Department of Social Services report puts the number at 303, the Department of Prisons recorded 299 children as of April 26, 2024.
Deepa believes the discrepancy will become clearer once the authorities concerned explain the differences in the reporting periods and calculation methods used in the two sets of data.

item.title: President calls for ensuring girls’ safety at home, in society and online

He made the remarks at a programme marking International and National Girl Child Day 2026 at the Bangladesh Shishu Academy auditorium on Monday.
The president said political commitment, administrative efficiency, social participation and, above all, a change in mindset were essential to empowering girls to achieve their full potential.
To prevent child marriage, the government is prioritising poverty alleviation, free education, stipends and stronger social safety nets, alongside verification of birth registrations and expanded opportunities for girls to pursue higher education, he said.
Referring to the killing of Tajmin, the president said: “We are moving forward, yet in some areas, we are regressing. It is the responsibility of guardians to look after their children. The girl from Cumilla was missing from home for three days, yet no concern was evident among her guardians.”
On public safety, he said: “When mothers sit on spread-out newspapers near schools waiting to take their children home, it reveals just how unsafe society has become.”

item.title: PM seeks Canadian support in energy, agriculture, climate finance
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday sought Canadian support in energy, agriculture and climate finance, while stressing the safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of around 1.3 million Rohingyas to Myanmar as the only sustainable solution to the crisis.
He made the call when a Canadian delegation, led by its Secretary of State (International Development) Randeep Sarai, met him at his office at the Secretariat.
The meeting discussed strengthening bilateral relations, expanding economic cooperation and exploring new opportunities for a strategic partnership between Bangladesh and Canada, said PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
Other key issues included technical and vocational education, food security, poverty alleviation and renewable energy.
On the Rohingya crisis, Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh is hosting around 1.3 million Rohingyas, putting considerable pressure on the country’s economy and environment while it continues to address its own economic and social challenges.
He said humanitarian assistance for the displaced people remained important, but their safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation is the only sustainable solution to the crisis, which originated in Myanmar and must be resolved there.
Randeep Sarai agreed on the importance of ensuring the peaceful, safe and dignified repatriation of Rohingyas.
The Canadian side expressed interest in cooperating with Bangladesh on energy supplies, particularly oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), saying Canada could be a potential partner in these areas.
Bangladesh said it will consider the proposal positively.
Canada expressed interest in expanding cooperation in technical and vocational education and training (TVET) in Bangladesh.
The two sides also discussed cooperation in establishing nursing training institutions and developing skilled nurses. Canada already has activities in this sector and plans to expand them further, the meeting was told.
The meeting discussed opportunities to strengthen cooperation in the production and supply of agricultural commodities, including pulses and oilseeds.
Canada expressed interest in supporting Bangladesh’s efforts to ensure food security.
The Prime Minister was also briefed on existing programmes being implemented through the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT).
The two sides also discussed Bangladesh’s Farmers’ Card programme, under which the government plans to provide farmers with essential agricultural inputs, including fertiliser and seeds.
Tarique Rahman said the programme will help the government maintain detailed information on farmers, enabling better agricultural planning and more effective delivery of public support.
The meeting discussed how Bangladesh could benefit from Canada’s experience in data management and evidence-based planning in this sector.
Referring to World Bank data, the Prime Minister said integrating multiple food subsidy programmes, improving the aims of existing cash assistance schemes and linking them with the Family Card could help lift an additional 2.85 million people out of poverty.
He stressed the importance of economic self-reliance, saying his government is focusing not only on social protection but also on expanding income and employment opportunities to help people become self-sufficient.
The meeting discussed Bangladesh’s renewable energy initiatives, canal excavation and the programme to plant 250 million trees.
Randeep Sarai said Canada is interested in providing C$13 billion in global climate finance over the next five years, noting that Bangladesh could benefit from the funding.
Canada also expressed interest in supporting feasibility studies for development projects in Bangladesh.
The Canadian secretary of state praised Bangladeshis and people of Bangladeshi origin living in Canada for their initiative, skills and positive outlook.
He also informed the Prime Minister that two people of Bangladeshi origin are serving as members of the Canadian Parliament.
At the end of the meeting, Sarai invited Tarique Rahman to visit Canada.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Education, Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Mahdi Amin, Press Secretary Saleh Shibly and relevant officials attended the meeting.
Canadian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Ajit Singh and senior officials from the Canadian side were also present.

item.title: Bangladesh seeks stronger energy ties with Saudi Arabia, Qatar
item.description:
Bangladesh has sought stronger energy cooperation with Saudi Arabia and Qatar while exploring foreign investment opportunities in its renewable energy sector during a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the 17th International Energy Forum held in Riyadh.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit held separate meetings with Saudi Assistant Minister of Energy for Electricity Nasser bin Hadi Al-Qahtani, Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs and Qatar Energy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, and ACWA Power CEO Dr Samir J Serhan, according to a message received on Monday.
The discussions focused on strengthening Bangladesh's energy security, securing long-term liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies, expanding bilateral cooperation and attracting foreign investment in renewable energy.
During his meeting with Saudi Assistant Minister Nasser Al-Qahtani, Amit expressed condolences over the deaths caused by a Houthi rebel attack at Riyadh International Airport and condemned the attack. He reaffirmed the solidarity of the government and people of Bangladesh with Saudi Arabia and briefed the Saudi official on the condolence message sent by Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to the Saudi crown prince and prime minister.
The Bangladesh state minister also sought Saudi Arabia's assistance in repatriating the bodies of two Bangladeshi nationals killed in the attack and ensuring medical treatment for those injured.
On energy cooperation, Amit sought Saudi support to strengthen Bangladesh's energy security. In response, the Saudi official described Bangladesh as a brotherly country that holds special importance for the Saudi government and expressed optimism about further expanding ongoing cooperation in energy security and other development initiatives.
The two sides stressed exchanging delegations and establishing a framework for understanding to discuss areas of Saudi support for Bangladesh's efforts to achieve its energy targets by 2030.
The discussions also covered long-term energy cooperation, the development of floating LNG terminals, and offshore and onshore gas exploration.
In his meeting with Qatar's State Minister for Energy Affairs Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Amit discussed Bangladesh's growing demand for natural gas, its existing LNG import arrangements and the possibility of signing new long-term supply agreements.
The two sides also explored LNG supplies from Qatar Energy's international portfolio and the diversification of supply sources and routes to strengthen Bangladesh's energy security. Both ministers stressed the need for continuing commercial and technical discussions between the relevant organisations.
In a third meeting, ACWA Power CEO Dr Samir J Serhan discussed investment opportunities in Bangladesh's renewable energy sector with the state minister. ACWA Power expressed interest in investing in the country's renewable energy sector.
Officials from the Bangladesh delegation and the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh were present at the meetings.

item.title: War and peace
item.description:
On the evening of February 24, 2022, I was due to teach an internal medicine session to a group of junior colleagues, among them a young physician from Ukraine.
She could not speak through her tears, and could not attend. Russian tanks had crossed her country's border hours earlier. I remember the silence on that call more clearly than almost anything said in it.
On the morning of October 7, 2023, I woke early and watched, in something close to real time, young people being dragged away from a music festival in southern Israel, and the destruction, within hours, of the Israeli villages bordering Gaza. Within perhaps half a day, hundreds were dead.
In the months since October 7, 2023, I have watched, night after night, as Gaza was reduced to rubble, hospitals bombed to ashes, and aid workers killed while children ran toward soup kitchens holding out bent and broken utensils, while white-painted drones circled overhead and IDF mortars piercing the sky above the blue Mediterranean.
And this year, a third conflict opened before I had recovered from the second: Iran and the United States, missiles fired across the Gulf, Saudi Arabia itself struck by Iranian fire meant for someone else.
Three theatres. Three of the most technologically advanced militaries in human history, deploying precision munitions, autonomous drones, and missile-defense systems worth billions of dollars.
And the result, in every case, is not zero. It is sub-zero.
More dead than before the shooting started. No peace concluded. No side visibly deterred.
Gaza in ruins. Ukraine still waiting for an end no one can date. The Gulf still bracing for the war's next act.
I have carried this fear since I was young enough to watch the towers fall in New York in 2001 -- nearly live, on the BBC, in the hospital corridor where I was on duty.
A nurse burst through the door, breathless, calling out my name twice -- “Rajani! Rajani!” -- as though the news itself could not wait for a full sentence. Some planes, she said, had struck the roof of a tower in New York.
Even Swedish radio, usually so measured, could not yet decipher what was happening, and for a long moment neither could we, standing together in that corridor, disbelieving.
And the tragic aftermath of nearly two decades of war that followed -- in Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan -- still haunts a generation of women denied their schooling, wrapped head to foot in black, in Kabul and elsewhere, in what was once a more modern country.
Weeks, months later, came a similar news alert: Netanyahu had ordered civilians in southern Lebanon to flee before a bombing spree. That same evening, sharing this over dinner with a friend, I found myself asking aloud what would happen if Putin attacked Sweden and told us to flee.
Flee where? For one unsettling moment, I did not want to know whether I was Lebanese, or Swedish, or a Bengali. I was simply a disposable object, waiting to be thrown into the trash of human folly.
And where does the Iran-US war fit into this -- a war still ongoing, its fragile ceasefires broken. I think here of a friend's son, married to an Iranian physician. On at least two occasions, she has flown to Sweden from elsewhere in the EU -- and each time, within days, as though summoned by some cruel and uncanny clock, a new round of bombing has broken out between the US and Iran.
I have joked with her, half-seriously by now: Whenever you are in Sweden, the US bombs Iran. But behind the joke sits something that is not funny at all -- her parents, still in Tehran, waiting out each night not knowing whether the next siren is the one that finally reaches them. Safe, so far. Only so far.
High technology has changed how efficiently human beings can kill one another. It has not changed why we do it, and it has not once, in any of these three wars, produced the thing weapons are supposedly for: Peace.
On August 7, 2026, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement in the city for which it is named -- a pact declaring that an armed attack on any one signatory will be treated as an attack on all three.
Commentators have already nicknamed it a “Sunni NATO,” though it has none of NATO's command structure, and its own foreign ministers insist it targets no one.
It was born, transparently, from the last 18 months: Saudi Arabia absorbing Iranian missile fire, Gulf states losing confidence that Washington will backstop their security in real time.
What concerns me is not the pact itself -- sovereign nations may organize their own defense as they judge wisest.
What concerns me is what comes next. Bangladeshi officials have confirmed that Saudi Arabia has invited Dhaka to consider joining. A junior foreign minister has called the idea something Bangladesh “views positively.” Nothing is decided. But the invitation is real, and so is the danger it opens.
Bangladesh has no quarrel with Iran. It has no stake in the Gulf. But under a mutual-defense clause, an attack on any member becomes everyone's war -- and Bangladesh's two nearest neighbours are nuclear-armed and have fought each other four times since 1947. The Radcliffe Line still runs raw through this region's memory.
Let me say plainly what I am not saying, because in this country, a byline is often read before an argument is. My surname will be filed by some readers, reflexively, as Hindu, and from there as pro-Indian -- a conflation as old and as unjust as the Radcliffe Line itself.
I write none of this out of sympathy for India over Pakistan, or Pakistan over India. I do not want Bangladesh dragged into a war against India, and I do not want it dragged into a war against Iran on Saudi Arabia's behalf, for exactly the same reason: I am against every war, everywhere, without exception, and I do not believe any Bangladeshi, of any faith, gains anything from a grave.
I say this as someone whose mother still lives in Dhaka, and who has, by his own choice, become something other than only Bangladeshi. Sweden is my home now.
I have watched Gaza's children, Tehran's children, and Ukraine's children -- and a Ukrainian doctor unable to speak through her tears -- with the same grief, because I claim no side except the side of those who did not choose any of it.
If Bangladesh is pulled into a war between India and Pakistan or over a Gulf dispute it never chose, the only outcome will be death -- Bangladeshi death, achieving nothing for Bangladesh.
There is a class of victims in these wars that rarely makes the front page, and I have not been able to stop thinking about them.
When the fighting between Iran and the United States widened into the Gulf this year, I watched footage of a drone strike setting fire to fuel tanks near Dubai International Airport -- an airport I have passed through so many times on my way to Dhaka or elsewhere that I could not, at first, quite believe what I was seeing.
What frightened me most, though, was not the airport. It was the millions of people from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and India who live and work across the Gulf states -- the drivers, nurses, construction workers, and domestic staff whose labour keeps those economies running, and whose remittances keep millions of families afloat back home.
Human rights organizations have already confirmed that Bangladeshi, Pakistani, and Nepali workers were killed in strikes on Gulf cities during this war -- a driver, a security guard, a water-tanker operator, ordinary people who chose this war no more than the residents of Gaza or Kharkiv did. In fact, two Bangladeshis were killed in the recent attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on October 10.
Had the fighting widened rather than paused, the danger to those workers would not have been only physical. It would also have been the danger of unemployment overnight -- a war turning millions of already vulnerable labourers into returnees with no income and no plan, in economies that cannot easily absorb them.
That fear sat in me with exactly the same weight as watching Gaza's children run toward a soup kitchen. A migrant worker killed in Dubai and a starving child in Gaza are not different categories of grief. They are the same failure, wearing different clothes.
Even the world's richest and most powerful nation cannot make the arithmetic of modern weaponry work.
A single Patriot interceptor takes years to build. The United States, still the strongest military and economic power on Earth, is nonetheless carrying a national debt now near forty trillion dollars, growing by billions of dollars every single day.
If a country of that wealth and scale cannot spend its way to peace through weapons, what should a country like Bangladesh conclude?
And this is not a hypothetical question for Bangladesh. Dhaka has recently advanced a deal to buy up to two dozen Chinese J-10CE fighter jets, at a cost reported near $2bn -- one of the largest defense procurements in the country's history.
Reasonable people can debate whether Bangladesh needs to modernize its air force. Probably it does. But before any such sum is committed, its politicians owe the public more than a single moment's reflection. They owe it a dozen.
What could two billion dollars buy in hospitals, schools, flood defenses, for a country that still struggles to fund all three?
Every taka spent on a fighter jet is a taka that cannot feed a child, treat a patient, or build a seawall against the rising water that will, with rising certainty, arrive before any invading army does.
This is the part of the ledger the war planners never show. Every high-tech weapon is a bet that violence, or the credible threat of it, will purchase something -- territory, deterrence, security, victory.
Three live wars, watched in real time by the whole world, have now tested that bet at unprecedented scale and technological sophistication. In every case, the bet has lost. Not broken even. Lost. No child's death has ever repaired a balance sheet. No missile fired has ever paid down a debt.
I write none of this from resentment toward the United States. I say this as a physician whose own career would not exist in its present form without America -- its conferences, its training programs, its medical journals and universities, the sheer excellence of its scientific culture.
I admire it, unreservedly, and I want it strong. That is exactly why watching its finances stretched thin by war, and its own missile stockpiles too depleted to properly defend an ally, causes me grief rather than any satisfaction.
A country I admire should not have to choose between its own future and one more interceptor.
I once spent six months working in Riyadh, and I still remember flying in and out of that city, looking down at a skyline that had not existed within living memory, and wondering, honestly, how it had been built.
Decades earlier, as a PhD student, I had discussed something similar with younger Swedish colleagues -- what people then called the postwar Western miracle: How ruined economies had rebuilt themselves not through conquest but through trade, institutions, and the free movement of people, capital, and ideas.
What I saw from the air over Riyadh, and later over Doha and Dubai, struck me as a second version of the same miracle: Glass towers and universities and airports risen from the desert within two generations, built by planning and investment rather than war.
Whatever one thinks of how that wealth arrived, its existence is a genuine human achievement -- proof that peace, prosperity, human mobility, and the free flow of capital and information are what progress actually looks like, in the Gulf as much as in the West.
None of it was built by weapons. All of it is now, in different ways, being asked to live under weapons' shadow.
That is the deeper waste: Not merely the money spent on armaments, but the fact that it is being subtracted from precisely the kinds of projects -- scientific, medical, economic, civic -- that have actually made nations great.
As a physician, I cannot stop thinking of it in those terms: Every fighter jet and every interceptor is money that did not go toward cancer research, or the next Ebola outbreak, or the next pandemic we have not yet named.
We know, because we have watched it happen twice in this decade already, that we are not owed advance warning.
If there is a lesson buried in seventy years of failed deterrence, it is not military. It is political.
The only durable peace project of the modern era is the European Union -- a continent that fought itself to exhaustion twice in 30 years, and has not fought itself once since 1945.
As a result, a Dane can breakfast in Copenhagen, lunch in Vienna, and dine in Paris, crossing what used to be the most contested borders on Earth without a checkpoint in sight today.
No missile shield built that. Shared institutions did -- habits of coexistence, patiently assembled, chosen over and over rather than imposed once.
South Asia has never had its Schuman moment -- the 1950 declaration that first bound France’s and Germany’s coal and steel industries together and became the seed from which the European Union grew.
It should not need a war to go looking for one. But it could still choose, deliberately, to become the region that tried.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

Greener Garments Initiative, Jamuna Group sign agreement for 34 MWp rooftop solar
item.description:
Greener Garments Initiative (GGI) has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Jamuna Group to install 34 MWp of solar panels on the rooftops of Jamuna Group’s factories.
It is the largest operating expense (Opex) rooftop solar agreement in the commercial and industrial sector of its kind in Bangladesh to date.
The Opex agreement was signed on Thursday, October 8, at the Bestseller office in Gulshan, Dhaka.
Sumaiya Rozalin Islam, group director of Jamuna Group, and Nure Alam, chief executive officer of GGI, signed on behalf of their organizations.
GGI board chairman Willem Grimminck and GGI board director Sebastian Groh were also present at the event.
Also present from Jamuna Group were Engr AKM Kamal, senior general manager, utility; Saiful Islam, head of legal; and Golam Sorwar Mozomder, senior general manager, accounts and finance.
From GGI and SOLshare, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, chief technology officer, and Aziza Sultana Mukti, deputy CEO, also attended.
GGI will fully finance the rooftop solar plants. Its founding partner, SOLshare, will engineer, procure, and commission (EPC) them, then operate and maintain them for the next 20 years.
Jamuna Group will make no upfront investment and will pay for the electricity the systems produce.
Once running, the systems are expected to generate 46,000 MWh of clean electricity while cutting about 30,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions per year, roughly the amount absorbed by more than one million trees in a year.
Jamuna Group’s factories also produce for Bestseller, the global family-owned fashion company.
Running these factories on solar power supports Bestseller’s Scope 3 emission reductions, which are the emissions from its supply chain, and helps it source greener fashion.
“For manufacturers in Bangladesh, rooftop solar is a business decision. It helps factories meet EU requirements, strengthens their relationships with customers, lowers energy costs and gives them the power they need to keep production lines running,” commented Willem Grimminck, chairman of the board, GGI.
“With this partnership, our factories will run on cleaner power. Jamuna Group is committed to cutting carbon emissions and meeting the compliance standards of our buyers. This model supports us in doing both, and helps us stay competitive as an exporter”, said Sumaiya Rozalin Islam, group director of Jamuna Group.
“Solar is where we start, but GGI offers a range of decarbonization solutions for factories, including battery storage, heat recovery, energy efficiency and water treatment. We take care of the cleaner energy and decarbonization side, so manufacturers can cut emissions across their whole operation and stay focused on their core business. We are ready to work with more factories in Bangladesh that want to make the same move,” added Nure Alam, CEO of GGI.

He is a resident student of Room 110 in Block A of the hall. Despite attempts to contact him, his whereabouts remain unknown.
A general diary was filed at Savar police station, and Dhaka District Superintendent of Police Shamima Parvin was informed of the incident.

item.title: Sadaqat, Imran help Pakistan thump Sri Lanka to seal T20 series
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat just missed out on a hundred as Pakistan upstaged Sri Lanka by 82 runs in the second T20 international on Sunday, taking an unbeatable 2-0 lead in the series.
Sadaqat's 51-ball 96 and Sahibzada Farhan's 44-ball 73 helped Pakistan to their highest T20 total at home of 215-3 in Rawalpindi.
Medium pacer Mohammad Imran then grabbed 3-11 to restrict Sri Lanka to 133-7 for Pakistan's biggest T20 win over the tourists.
Sri Lanka lost wickets at regular intervals with Maheesh Theekshana (32 not out) and Chamindu Wickramasinghe (29) offering some resistance once the game was beyond reach.
Kamindu Mendis (23) and Sineth Jayawardena (22) were the only others to reach double figures.
Pakistan benefited from three dropped catches by Sri Lanka as Sadaqat and Farhan punished the attack, adding 88 runs for the second wicket off just 49 balls.
Sadaqat smashed seven sixes -- the joint most by a Pakistan batter in a T20s -- and six fours before being dismissed off the final delivery of the innings.
Farhan, dropped on two and 11, hit five sixes and four fours before he holed out to Dasun Shanaka in the 15th over.
Sadaqat, who was put down on 44, then cut loose and added a quickfire 72 off 31 balls for the third wicket with Hasan Nawaz (19 not out).
Pakistan plundered 70 runs in the last five overs, improving on their highest home T20 total of 208-3 against the West Indies in Karachi five years ago.
The third and final match is on Tuesday.
